title: How to Lead When the Path Isn’t Clear
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that when a team faces an unclear path, the useful move is to ask good questions rather than rush to answers or wait for certainty. She contrasts momentum makers, who generate forward motion and alignment through inquiry, with momentum takers who wait for someone else to clear the fog. She offers a four-part skillset of observation, reframing, sequencing and exploration, with concrete example questions for each. She then ties the approach to Situational Leadership, Marquet, Dweck and Senge, which all stress inquiry over having every answer. The piece closes with reflection prompts urging leaders to start with a question the next time they face uncertainty.
points: Uncertainty becomes dangerous when teams either rush to satisfying but weak answers or wait for complete information and never start.
Momentum makers use questions such as what the real decision is, what is known and unknown, and what is under the team's control to turn stuck meetings into action.
The four practices are noticing friction, turning judgments into hypotheses, asking in layers from tangible to abstract, and reviewing which questions went unasked.
Asking what is happening before asking why keeps inquiry from stalling on big abstract questions.
The author situates the habit within Situational Leadership, Leader-Leader, Growth Mindset and Senge's systems thinking.
quotes: Some people look for answers, whereas others start asking questions. And the difference is huge… Because when you’re in a fuzzy space - messy, unscripted, full of half-formed ideas - clarity doesn’t come from certainty, but from inquiry.
We like to imagine that leadership involves moving along a clear track. Strategy defines the way forward. The team executes. Progress follows.
Momentum makers don’t force clarity where there is none. But they don’t freeze either. They ask questions that generate forward motion and alignment.
Big, abstract questions stall progress. The best insights come from well-sequenced inquiry: start with the tangible, then zoom out. Ask what’s happening (and truly listen!) before asking why.
Turn judgments into hypotheses. Change “We’re too slow” into “Where is speed actually required?” Shift “Nobody gets it” into “What assumptions are we making about their context?

Each model reinforces that effective leadership isn’t about having all the answers, but about guiding teams through uncertainty by focusing on the right inquiries, which ultimately drives better decision-making and long-term success.
